newsitem.title: USA: Russia wins seat at G7 table, except on finances.
newsitem.headline: Russia wins seat at G7 table, except on finances.

text.p: When G7 leaders reached out to Mikhail Gorbachev in the Soviet Union's waning days, they invited him to their 1991 London summit -- but only for lunch.

Six years later his successor, Russian President Boris Yeltsin, will take part in every meal and meeting at next week's Group of Seven (G7) summit in Denver except one, a Saturday afternoon session on economic and financial issues.
That evolution shows how far Russia has come since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991 as well as the distance it will have to go before its economy will gain a full seat at the G7.

U.S. officials, hosts for the June 20-22 summit, say Russia's expanded role at Denver is justified by its weight in the world and argue that its presence serves the interests of the leading industrial nations, as well as of Russia itself.
On matters from fighting global crime and terror to promoting nuclear safety and non-proliferation, they said, Russia's active collaboration was vital.

"It's impossible to imagine working on those issues without Russia," said one official. "The philosophy that drives this process is that if you bring them in at the early stages, it's easier to get them around to your side of the table."
"Increased Russian participation is a benefit to the seven as well as to Russia," said another U.S.official. "We really regard this as a win-win situation."
Cooperation on political matters has been the rule since Soviet and Russian leaders began coming to the meetings, at one point leading to talk of a "P8" group on political issues.

At Denver, however, Yeltsin's participation will go beyond this and he will join in talks on selected economic matters, such as how to cope with ageing populations and how to design social safety nets to serve them.

Some analysts view Russia's enhanced role as a reward for its grudging acceptance of the planned advance of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) into Eastern Europe, although U.S. officials say the two matters were not linked.
In a rhetorical effort to underscore Russia's expanded participation, the United States has baptised the Denver meeting the "Summit of the Eight."

The one meeting from which Russia will be excluded is a Saturday afternoon session focusing on the core G7 economic issues -- a discussion of exchange rates and monetary policy that in some years has made world financial markets tremble.
But giving Russia a greater role in the G7 has not been met with unqualified praise.

"It is very good that the summit should be used to integrate the Russians into the global system, to demonstrate that we recognise their economic and political reforms and that they are a major player," said Robert Hormats, vice chairman of investment bank Goldman Sachs International.

"But I think it is important that the G7 not lose its focus on its role as the pre-eminent institution on maintaining a strong, open-market, financial, monetary and trading system," he added. "There is a danger of losing that sense of responsibility for the global system."

And not all G7 members were initially enthusiastic about Russia's inclusion. Japan, for example, at first opposed it before changing its mind, apparently deciding that continued opposition might hurt its improving ties with Moscow.

In particular, the Japanese are keen to resolve a territorial dispute with Russia over four Pacific islands, and Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto is expected to raise the matter with Yeltsin on the sidelines of the G7 meeting.

Russia has also been pressing for membership in a host of other Western institutions, including the Paris Club of creditor nations, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development and the World Trade Organisation.

Of the three, the only one that Moscow is close to joining is the Paris Club, although a senior U.S. official suggested this week that negotiations over this were unlikely to be wrapped up in time to make an announcement at Denver.

One senior U.S. official suggested that binding Russia more tightly to the G7 also had a psychological benefit by helping Russians see themselves as part of the wider world they once faced from behind the Iron Curtain.
"Ultimately this process...is giving them the opportunity to promote and advance their own interests in concert with us, rather than having to define themselves in opposition to us," he said.
